final_writeup:
The target remains unresolved, but the following self-contained bounds and reduction were obtained. Writing μ_n=E theta(G_n),

sqrt(n)+(n+1-2sqrt(n))/2^(n choose 2) <= μ_n <= (2+o(1))sqrt(n).

Consequently 1 <= liminf μ_n/sqrt(n) <= limsup μ_n/sqrt(n) <= 2. Moreover theta(G_n) lies between (1/2-o(1))sqrt(n) and (2+o(1))sqrt(n) with probability tending to one. The upper bound comes from an explicit signed-matrix SDP dual certificate and a trace-moment comparison with a Gaussian matrix; no external random-matrix theorem is assumed without a proof argument.

There is also an exact diagnosis of the remaining gap. If T_n=theta(G_n) and T_n^c=theta(complement(G_n)), then

μ_n-sqrt(n) = (1/2) E[(sqrt(T_n)-sqrt(T_n^c))^2] + E[sqrt(T_n T_n^c)-sqrt(n)].

Using the proved upper tail and product-measure correlation, the first term is o(sqrt(n)) exactly when Var(T_n)=o(n). Thus the conjectured limit 1 is equivalent to two concrete assertions: sublinear variance and asymptotic saturation in expectation of theta(G_n)theta(complement(G_n)) >= n. Neither assertion is established here, so this is a partial result rather than a proof of the requested limit.

results.claim: For every graph H, theta(H)=min lambda_max(M), where M ranges over real symmetric matrices satisfying M_ii=1 and M_ij=1 for every distinct nonedge ij of H. Also 1 <= theta(H) <= |V(H)|.
results.proof_sketch: Dualizing the defining SDP gives min t subject to tI-M positive semidefinite, with entries of M fixed to those of the all-ones matrix except on edges, where they are free. The primal point I/|V(H)| is positive definite and satisfies every edge constraint, so strong duality applies; eliminating t gives the formula. A one-coordinate diagonal matrix is primal-feasible and has objective 1. Conversely, J <= |V(H)|I in positive-semidefinite order, so <J,X> <= |V(H)| Tr(X)=|V(H)|.

results.claim: If μ_n=E theta(G_n) and N=binom(n,2), then μ_n >= sqrt(n)+(n+1-2sqrt(n))/2^N; in particular μ_n>sqrt(n) for every n>1.
results.proof_sketch: The supplied complement inequality gives theta(H)theta(complement(H)) >= n, hence theta(H)+theta(complement(H)) >= 2sqrt(n). Complementation pairs the 2^N labeled graphs, and G_n and its complement have the same law, yielding μ_n>=sqrt(n). For the empty/complete pair, the two theta values are n and 1, so its sum exceeds the generic lower bound by n+1-2sqrt(n). Retaining this exact excess while using 2sqrt(n) for every other pair proves the displayed inequality.

results.claim: Let Z be symmetric with zero diagonal and independent standard Gaussian entries above the diagonal. For every integer k>=1, (E lambda_max(Z)^(2k))^(1/(2k)) <= 2sqrt(n)+2sqrt(k).
results.proof_sketch: For unit x, set X_x=x^T Zx. Direct calculation gives E(X_x-X_y)^2 <= 4(1-(x·y)^2) <= 8(1-x·y). For Y_x=2g·x with g standard Gaussian, the last expression equals E(Y_x-Y_y)^2. Gaussian interpolation on a finite sphere net—differentiate the expected log-sum-exp and use Gaussian integration by parts—therefore gives E sup_x X_x <= E sup_x Y_x=2E||g||<=2sqrt(n); taking finer nets proves E lambda_max(Z)<=2sqrt(n). The map from the independent Gaussian entries to lambda_max(Z) is sqrt(2)-Lipschitz. The Gaussian exponential-moment argument obtained from integration by parts gives P(lambda_max(Z)-E lambda_max(Z)>=t)<=exp(-t^2/4). Integrating this tail shows the 2k-th norm of its positive deviation is at most 2sqrt(k), and Minkowski's inequality proves the claim.

results.claim: Let W be symmetric with zero diagonal and independent uniform signs above the diagonal. For every integer k>=1, E lambda_max(W) <= (2n)^(1/(2k))(2sqrt(n)+2sqrt(k)).
results.proof_sketch: Expand Tr(W^(2k)) as a sum over closed walks. A loop-free walk has nonzero Rademacher expectation exactly when every unoriented edge occurs an even number of times, in which case its expectation is 1. For the Gaussian matrix Z, the same walk contributes the product over used edges of (m_e-1)!!, which is at least 1. Hence E Tr(W^(2k)) <= E Tr(Z^(2k)) term by term. If L=lambda_max(Z), then Tr(Z^(2k)) <= n(L^(2k)+lambda_max(-Z)^(2k)); symmetry and the preceding Gaussian bound give E Tr(Z^(2k)) <= 2n(2sqrt(n)+2sqrt(k))^(2k). Finally lambda_max(W)^(2k) <= Tr(W^(2k)), and the power-mean inequality yields the result.

results.claim: For every k>=1 and a>0, E theta(G_n) <= 1+(2n)^(1/(2k))(2sqrt(n)+2sqrt(k)), and P(theta(G_n)>1+a) <= 2n((2sqrt(n)+2sqrt(k))/a)^(2k). Consequently E theta(G_n) <= (2+o(1))sqrt(n), and for each fixed epsilon>0 the probability theta(G_n)>(2+epsilon)sqrt(n) is exp(-Omega_epsilon((log n)^2)).
results.proof_sketch: Put W_ij=1 on nonedges and -1 on edges. Then W has independent signs, while M=I+W has diagonal and nonedge entries equal to 1. The dual formula therefore gives theta(G_n)<=1+lambda_max(W). Apply the preceding expectation bound. For the tail, Markov's inequality applied to Tr(W^(2k)) gives the displayed estimate. Taking k=ceil((log n)^2) makes (2n)^(1/(2k))=1+o(1) and sqrt(k)=o(sqrt(n)); the same choice makes the fixed-epsilon tail superpolynomially small.

results.claim: For every fixed epsilon>0, P((1/2-epsilon)sqrt(n) <= theta(G_n) <= (2+epsilon)sqrt(n)) tends to 1.
results.proof_sketch: The upper assertion is the preceding tail bound. Apply that bound also to the identically distributed complement. On the event theta(complement(G_n)) <= (2+delta)sqrt(n), the supplied product inequality forces theta(G_n) >= sqrt(n)/(2+delta). Choose delta>0 so that 1/(2+delta)>1/2-epsilon.

results.claim: If H is obtained by deleting one vertex from G, then theta(H) <= theta(G) <= theta(H)+1. Consequently Var(theta(G_n)) <= (n-1)/4 and P(|theta(G_n)-μ_n|>=t) <= 2exp(-2t^2/(n-1)).
results.proof_sketch: Padding a feasible matrix for H with a zero row and column proves the first inequality. For the second, write a feasible matrix for G as the Gram matrix of vectors b_v and b_i, and put q=||b_v||^2 and s=sum_{i!=v}b_i. The restricted block has trace 1-q, so ||s||^2 <= (1-q)theta(H). Thus the objective is at most (sqrt(q)+sqrt((1-q)theta(H)))^2 <= 1+theta(H). Generate G_n from n-1 independent blocks, block i containing all edges from i to earlier vertices. Replacing one block changes only edges incident to one vertex, hence changes theta by at most 1. The bounded-difference martingale gives the stated tail; summing its conditional variances, each at most 1/4, gives the variance bound.

results.claim: With T_n=theta(G_n), T_n^c=theta(complement(G_n)), and μ_n=E T_n, the exact identity μ_n-sqrt(n)=(1/2)E[(sqrt(T_n)-sqrt(T_n^c))^2]+E[sqrt(T_n T_n^c)-sqrt(n)] holds, and both terms on the right are nonnegative.
results.proof_sketch: The two variables have the same expectation. Expanding the square makes the right side equal to (1/2)E[T_n+T_n^c-2sqrt(T_nT_n^c)]+E[sqrt(T_nT_n^c)]-sqrt(n)=μ_n-sqrt(n). The square is nonnegative, and the second summand is pointwise nonnegative by the supplied complement inequality.

results.claim: The target limit μ_n/sqrt(n)->1 is equivalent to the conjunction Var(T_n)=o(n) and E[sqrt(T_nT_n^c)-sqrt(n)]=o(sqrt(n)).
results.proof_sketch: The exact identity first shows that the limit is equivalent to the product-slack condition and S_n:=E[(sqrt(T_n)-sqrt(T_n^c))^2]=o(sqrt(n)). It remains to identify S_n. If Var(T_n)=o(n), then E(T_n-T_n^c)^2<=4Var(T_n), while (sqrt(x)-sqrt(y))^2<=|x-y|; hence S_n=o(sqrt(n)). Conversely fix C>2. The proved tail makes P(max(T_n,T_n^c)>Csqrt(n)) superpolynomially small. On the complementary event, (T_n-T_n^c)^2 <=4Csqrt(n)(sqrt(T_n)-sqrt(T_n^c))^2; using T_n,T_n^c<=n handles the exceptional event, so S_n=o(sqrt(n)) implies E(T_n-T_n^c)^2=o(n). Finally T_n decreases and T_n^c increases in every independent edge indicator. The elementary product-measure correlation inequality (proved by induction over indicators) gives Cov(T_n,T_n^c)<=0, whence E(T_n-T_n^c)^2>=2Var(T_n). Thus Var(T_n)=o(n).
